title: Can you structure these 13 cost reduction case questions in two minutes each?
description: 13 cost reduction case prompts to structure in two minutes each, with model answers, where to start and the trap to avoid.
hook: Cost prompts are about discipline: biggest lines first, and never cut what brings in revenue. Give yourself two minutes per prompt, then open the model and look for what you missed.
body:
1. A fashion retailer's online returns now cost $40M a year, double three years ago.

Show a model structure
  • Number of returns: Online orders: did sales grow?; Return rate by category, size, brand; serial returners
  • Cost per return: Shipping, handling, refurbishing; Items that can no longer be sold
  • Why customers return: Fit and sizing, photos and descriptions; Ordering several sizes on purpose
  • Policy: Free returns, return window; Charging, store returns, exchanges first

Where to start: Orders × return rate × cost per return: find which grew, then the categories driving it.

The trap: Listing policies to change without first splitting the number of returns from cost per return.

2. A retail bank wants to cut operating costs by 15% in two years.

Show a model structure
  • Branches: Number, size and use of branches; Staffing vs footfall
  • Operations: Back office: payments, lending, account opening; Automation and outsourcing
  • Technology: Old systems, licences, data centres; Duplicate apps and vendors
  • Support functions: HR, finance, procurement; Spans of control and layers

Where to start: The biggest cost pool first: usually staff in branches and operations.

The trap: Listing cost ideas without sizing the cost base, so you can't say which matters.

3. A food-delivery start-up is burning $5M a month. Where would you cut?

Show a model structure
  • Unit economics per order: Commission, delivery fee, courier cost; Discounts and refunds
  • Marketing: Cost to acquire a customer vs their value; Promotions with no repeat
  • Cities: Profit by city; Exit or pause the weakest
  • Fixed costs: Head office, tech, offices; Hiring plans

Where to start: Profit per order by city: losing money on every order can't be fixed with volume.

The trap: Cutting head office first when the loss is in every order.

4. A bakery chain throws away 15% of what it bakes.

Show a model structure
  • What is wasted: By product, store and day; Fresh vs packaged
  • Forecasting: How stores decide how much to bake; Weather, events, promotions
  • Ordering and production: Batch sizes, minimum orders; Baking once vs through the day
  • Selling it off: End-of-day discounts, donations; Apps for surplus food

Where to start: Forecasting: most waste comes from baking for the best day every day.

The trap: Cutting the range before fixing how much is baked.

5. An energy supplier's unpaid bills have doubled.

Show a model structure
  • Who is not paying: Customer segment, payment method; New vs long-standing customers
  • Why: Higher bills, cost of living; Billing errors, estimated readings
  • Collections: How quickly we chase; Payment plans offered
  • Prevention: Prepayment and smart meters; Credit checks when joining

Where to start: Who is not paying: hardship and billing errors need different responses.

The trap: Chasing harder without separating customers who can't pay from those who won't.

6. An online furniture retailer's delivery cost per order rose 40%.

Show a model structure
  • Orders: Order size and weight; Share of two-person deliveries
  • Routes: Drops per van per day; Distance between drops, rural share
  • Failures: Failed deliveries and returns; Damage in transit
  • Rates: Carrier prices, fuel; Own fleet vs third party

Where to start: Drops per van: density usually explains most of the cost per order.

The trap: Renegotiating carrier rates while failed deliveries keep rising.

7. Should a bank close a third of its branches?

Show a model structure
  • Usage: Visits and transactions per branch; Who still uses branches
  • Savings: Rent, staff, maintenance per branch; Closure costs
  • Customer impact: Customers who might leave; Vulnerable customers, rural areas
  • Alternatives: Shared branches, post offices; Mobile and video banking

Where to start: Usage: which branches have few visits and alternatives nearby.

The trap: Closing by cost alone without checking which customers would leave.

8. How can a hospital cut costs by 5% without harming patient care?

Show a model structure
  • Staff: Agency staff vs permanent; Rostering to demand
  • Supplies and drugs: Buying together, cheaper equivalents; Waste and stock
  • Patient flow: Length of stay, cancelled operations; Theatre utilisation
  • Estate and back office: Energy, buildings; Admin, IT

Where to start: Agency staff: usually the most expensive way to fill a shift.

The trap: Cutting front-line staff numbers instead of how they are used.

9. How could a supermarket chain cut its energy use by 20%?

Show a model structure
  • Refrigeration: Doors on fridges, efficient units; Maintenance and leaks
  • Lighting and heating: LEDs, controls; Heat recovered from fridges
  • Buildings: Insulation, solar panels; Store design
  • Behaviour and data: Smart meters per store; Targets and training

Where to start: Refrigeration: usually the biggest energy user in a supermarket.

The trap: Starting with lighting because it's easy.

10. How can a retailer cut theft and stock losses by half?

Show a model structure
  • Where losses happen: Stores, products, times; Theft vs errors vs damage
  • External theft: Security, tags, layout; Self-checkout controls
  • Internal: Staff theft, processes; Audits
  • Errors and damage: Deliveries, pricing, waste; Stock counting

Where to start: Where losses happen: a few stores and products usually account for most.

The trap: Adding guards everywhere.

11. A haulier's trucks run empty 30% of the time. How can it reduce that?

Show a model structure
  • Where empty miles happen: Return legs, regions, days; Customers with one-way flows
  • Find loads: Freight exchanges, partners; Sales to fill backhauls
  • Plan better: Route planning, combining loads; Depot locations
  • Price: Discounts for return loads; Contracts that pay for empty legs

Where to start: Where empty miles happen: return legs from a few lanes.

The trap: Buying planning software without customers to fill the trucks.

12. How can a hotel group cut costs by 10% without guests noticing?

Show a model structure
  • Staff: Rostering to occupancy; Shared roles across hotels
  • Rooms: Laundry, amenities, energy; Linen changes on longer stays
  • Food and drink: Menus, waste, suppliers; Breakfast set-up
  • Central costs: Buying together; Technology, marketing

Where to start: Staff rostered to occupancy: the biggest cost moves with demand.

The trap: Cutting things guests do notice, such as room quality.

13. How can a fashion retailer cut the stock it sells at discount from 40% to 25%?

Show a model structure
  • Buying: Fewer lines, smaller first orders; Better forecasts
  • Speed: Faster suppliers, repeat orders; Test before buying big
  • Allocation: Right sizes to the right stores; Moving stock between stores
  • Pricing: Smaller discounts given earlier; Outlets and resale

Where to start: Buying: most markdowns are decided when stock is ordered.

The trap: Focusing on clearance tactics instead of buying less.
